correctness.rationale: The primary source proves the standard 24-cell has 24 octahedral facets of 3-volume sqrt(2)/3 and four root normals for each coordinate pair. Applying Cauchy projection formula gives b(u)=sum_{i<j}(|u_i+u_j|+|u_i-u_j|)/3, hence b=2(3a1+2a2+a3)/3 for sorted absolute coordinates. Cauchy--Schwarz gives the sharp maximum sqrt(14), with only sorted normal (3,2,1,0)/sqrt(14), yielding exactly 192 signed permutations. For the minimum, decompose any sorted nonnegative vector into the four nested 0/1 coordinate generators. Their L/norm ratios are exactly (3,5/sqrt2,2sqrt3,3). Triangle inequality and its strict equality conditions give L>=3, with equality only at generator 1 or 4; hence exactly 8 coordinate-axis and 16 half-sign minimizing directions. Continuity gives the full interval; actual packaged rational checker verifies facet and normalization computations without being used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Full relevant sections of both accessible recent primary texts were inspected: they supply the 24-cell facet and dual-root data and establish isoperimetry/design structure, but not the exact four-dimensional brightness profile or two sharp equality sets. Searches in shadow volumes, projection bodies, root-zonotope support radii, and published records did not identify an equivalent classification. Potential older Coxeter-zonotope formulations remain the key residual originality risk; failure to find them is not treated as mathematical proof of novelty.
residual_risks: An older root-system, Weyl-zonotope, or polytope-projection reference may give the same extrema in different terminology despite the targeted searches.

No stability bound for approximately extremal projection directions is supplied.

value.rationale: The four-dimensional regular 24-cell is a natural extremal convex polytope, recently shown uniquely isoperimetric among translative tiles. Hyperplane shadow volume is a fundamental and physically interpretable directional invariant of a convex body. The theorem completely classifies its sharp anisotropy (ratio sqrt14/3), identifies the surprising coincidence of all 24 least-bright directions with the original 24 vertex rays, and determines the 192 most-bright directions with no unproved extremal cases. These sharp, normalized and geometry-motivated data are useful as a benchmark for geometric tomography and the study of projection bodies; no general theorem or publication-sized claim is necessary.
